analysis.one_liner: Blocks any new federal regulation from taking effect until Congress passes it as a law.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it got one subcommittee hearing in September 1996 and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, despite 58 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required every federal agency regulation to be enacted by Congress, as an ordinary bill signed by the President, before it could take effect. Agencies would submit the text of each new rule, and under expedited procedures each chamber would have to pass it within 60 days. Because agencies issue thousands of binding rules each year — on air and water quality, workplace safety, food safety, banking, and more — this would have effectively shut down federal rulemaking: rules Congress never got around to passing would simply never become law.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses and industries regulated by federal agencies would gain the most, since almost no new regulation could take effect without an act of Congress, and Congress could not realistically process the volume of rules agencies produce each year. The bill's backers framed the same change as a gain for the public: making elected lawmakers personally answerable for every federal rule instead of allowing 'unelected' agency officials to write them.

how_it_helps.text: No regulation could take effect until a bill made up solely of that regulation's text was enacted by Congress and signed by the President, ending the current system in which agency rules carry the force of law on their own.

The bill created fast-track procedures: the regulation's text would be introduced as a bill within three days, could not be sent to committee, would get one hour of debate, could not be amended, and had to receive an up-or-down vote within 60 calendar days.

Sponsors argued this would enforce Article I of the Constitution by ending the practice of Congress delegating lawmaking to executive-branch officials and requiring elected members to take responsibility for federal regulations.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal protections would bear the cost: clean air and water rules, workplace and food safety standards, and financial and consumer protections would lapse whenever Congress failed or declined to pass them. Federal agencies would lose their core function, and the public would lose the technical expertise and speed of the rulemaking process.

drawbacks.text: Agencies issue thousands of binding regulations each year; Congress historically cannot pass even hundreds of bills in a session, so most new rules would never be enacted and existing protections would erode by default.

The bill excluded only narrow categories (rules of particular applicability and interpretive or procedural rules), so every substantive safety, health, environmental, and financial rule would have needed a separate act of Congress.

Supporters had a serious good-faith point: Congress routinely delegates lawmaking to agencies whose officials face no voters, and the Constitution assigns legislative power to Congress. An honest supporter would acknowledge, though, that the fix as written traded accountability for near-total regulatory paralysis.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The accountability argument is real — agency officials answer to no voters, and Congress often hides behind the rules agencies write. But the remedy as designed would not have made Congress more accountable; it would have made regulation mostly impossible. A body that struggles to pass routine legislation could not affirmatively enact thousands of technical rules a year, so the predictable result was that protections for air, water, workplaces, food, and consumers would quietly disappear — a benefit flowing to regulated industries, not to the public the sponsors said they were protecting.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Judiciary and Rules Committees, sent to two subcommittees, got a single subcommittee hearing in September 1996, was never reported out of committee, and died when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. J.D. Hayworth introduced the bill on December 6, 1995, and it was referred to the Judiciary Committee and, in addition, the Rules Committee.

In early January 1996 it was referred to the Rules Committee's Subcommittee on Rules and Organization of the House, and in February 1996 to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law.

The only substantive action after that was a subcommittee hearing on September 12, 1996; the full committee never voted, and the House never considered the bill before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies kept their authority to issue binding regulations without a separate act of Congress, and the public kept the protections that flow from that rulemaking system. Businesses hoping regulation would be effectively shut down gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Agencies and people relying on federal rules

for.name: Rep. J.D. Hayworth
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it twice, in January and April 1996.

for.name: 55 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, joining 3 House Democrats among its 58 cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law, held one subcommittee hearing on September 12, 1996, and never reported the bill to the full House.

against.name: House Rules Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Rules and Organization of the House in January 1996 and took no further action on it.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 55 of the bill's 58 cosponsors were House Republicans, with 3 House Democrats joining.

industries.industry: Federally regulated businesses (polluters, employers, food and drug makers, financial firms)
industries.note: If no regulation could take effect without an act of Congress, new safety, health, environmental, and financial rules would largely stop, freeing regulated businesses from compliance costs at the public's expense.

Agencies would lose their core power to make rules carry the force of law, crippling their ability to enforce the statutes Congress has passed. Their loss would have been the public's loss on the same issues.
